questions.q: OLS, the spatial lag model and the spatial error model are all global models. What does that mean?
options: They use data from the whole world
They estimate one set of coefficients for the whole study area, assuming relationships are the same everywhere
They can only use areal data
questions.why: When processes are non-stationary, a single coefficient can hide how relationships change across space.

questions.q: How does GWR differ from OLS?
options: It estimates a separate regression at each location, so coefficients can vary across space
It uses a different outcome variable at each location
questions.why: Each local regression uses nearby observations, weighted by distance.

questions.q: GWR gives more weight to observations closer to the regression point. Which idea is this built on?
questions.why: Near things are more related than distant things, so nearby observations count more.

questions.q: Census tracts are small in cities and large in rural areas. Which bandwidth usually fits better?
options: A fixed bandwidth (the same distance everywhere)
An adaptive bandwidth (the same number of nearest neighbors everywhere)
questions.why: An adaptive bandwidth shrinks where observations are dense and grows where they are sparse.

questions.q: As the GWR bandwidth gets very large, the local estimates...
options: become smoother and approach the global OLS model
questions.why: A small bandwidth gives very local, possibly noisy estimates. A huge bandwidth uses nearly everything, which is just OLS.

questions.q: How is the GWR bandwidth usually chosen?
options: By hand, based on what looks best
By minimizing AICc or a cross-validation score
questions.why: The chosen bandwidth reflects the scale at which the process is assumed to operate.

questions.q: An area with a low local R² in a GWR may suggest...
options: an important variable is missing from the model in that area
the bandwidth is too large everywhere
questions.why: Local R² maps where the model explains the outcome well and where it doesn't.

questions.q: In the North Carolina example, the global coefficient for percent with a bachelor's degree is about $7,200, while local coefficients range from about $3,400 to $10,500. What does this show?
options: The global model is wrong about the sign
The relationship varies across the state, which a single coefficient hides
questions.why: This is non-stationarity: the same variable is associated with home value more strongly in some places than others.

questions.q: Which is a limitation of GWR?
options: Variables can be strongly correlated within a local neighborhood (local multicollinearity), making coefficients unstable
It only uses one observation per regression
questions.why: GWR is mainly exploratory. Coefficient variation could reflect a real process difference or a missing variable.

options: Each variable gets its own bandwidth, so some relationships can be local while others are close to global
questions.why: Standard GWR assumes every relationship operates at the same scale.

questions.q: In k-means clustering, two census tracts are "close" when...
options: they have similar values across all of the clustering variables (attribute space)
they're within 5 miles of each other
questions.why: Distance in k-means is measured in attribute space, not geographic space.

questions.q: Why are variables usually standardized into z-scores before k-means?
options: So variables on large scales, like income in dollars, don't dominate variables measured as percentages
questions.why: K-means uses distance, so a variable's units would otherwise decide how much it counts.

options: choose the number of clusters, k
questions.why: It plots within-cluster variation against k and looks for where more clusters stop helping much. The silhouette score and interpretability matter too.

questions.q: Why is k-means usually run many times with different random starting points?
options: Because the result depends on the starting centroids, so you keep the solution with the smallest within-cluster variation
questions.why: Different starting points can lead to different final clusters.

questions.q: K-means doesn't use location, yet the cluster map shows strong spatial patterns. Why?
options: The input variables are spatially dependent, so similar places tend to be near each other
questions.why: If you want clusters made only of neighboring areas, use spatially constrained clustering such as SKATER.

questions.q: Not every resident of a tract labeled "student neighborhood" is a student. This is the...
questions.why: A cluster describes the average characteristics of an area, not the individuals in it.
